title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
description: Brute force to optimized: generating every full parenthesization shape versus divide-and-conquer on substrings with memoization.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string expression of numbers and the operators "+", "-", and "*", return all possible results obtained by computing the expression with parentheses added in every possible way, grouping numbers and operators differently. The results may be returned in any order.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Every way of grouping/parenthesizing an expression\"","Divide and conquer: split at each operator, treating it as the LAST one applied, and combine results from both sides"],["Overlapping substrings recomputed across different splits","Memoization on the substring to avoid redundant recomputation"]]}

blocks.text: Every way of adding parentheses corresponds to choosing, at the TOP level, which operator is applied LAST (outermost). Splitting the expression at that operator divides it into a left substring and a right substring, each of which can itself be grouped in every possible way, recursively.

blocks.title: Analogy: Every Way to Total a Multi-Step Purchase
blocks.text: Picture a receipt combining several add, subtract, and multiply steps, and wanting every possible final total depending on which operation is considered "applied last" (like choosing to bracket different parts of a formula). This problem asks for every such possible final total.

blocks.caption: Trying every operator as the LAST one applied splits the expression into two independently-recursible halves

blocks.text: Result: [2, 0]. (2-1)-1 = 0, and 2-(1-1) = 2, giving these two distinct results.

Before generating every possible fully-parenthesized string and evaluating each, notice that choosing which operator is applied LAST is exactly what a parenthesization determines, and this choice naturally splits the expression into a left and right substring, each solvable by the exact same recursive process.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For any operator in the expression, imagining it as the LAST operation applied means everything to its left forms one sub-expression, and everything to its right forms another, each of which can independently be grouped in every possible way.

Observation 2: The set of possible results for the left substring, combined pairwise (using the chosen operator) with the set of possible results for the right substring, gives every result achievable with that operator as the outermost one.

Observation 3: Repeating this for EVERY operator position in the expression, and taking the union of all resulting values, covers every possible full parenthesization.

Observation 4: Many different splits can produce the SAME substring (for example, in longer expressions), so memoizing results by substring avoids redundant recomputation of identical subproblems.

This leads to recursively trying every operator as the last one applied, splitting into left and right substrings, recursing (with memoization) on each, and combining every pair of results with that operator.
Generate every possible fully-parenthesized version of the expression (as strings), then evaluate each one from scratch using an expression evaluator.

items: Enumerate every way to fully parenthesize the expression (every binary tree shape over the operators).
For each parenthesization, evaluate it directly following the explicit grouping.

codes.python:
# Conceptually: generate every possible binary tree shape over the operators
# (Catalan-number many shapes), build the corresponding fully-parenthesized
# expression for each, and evaluate it directly. Correct, but treats each
# shape independently, re-evaluating overlapping sub-expressions repeatedly
# instead of reusing their results.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Enumerating every full parenthesization shape directly mirrors the problem definition.
It does not reuse the result of evaluating a shared sub-expression across different overall shapes, doing redundant work.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: Catalan-number many shapes (exponential in the number of operators), each requiring evaluation.
Space: exponential, to store all generated shapes.
Limitation: different top-level splits can share identical substrings; recursing directly on substrings and memoizing results avoids re-deriving the same substring's possible values multiple times.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why generating full shapes explicitly is wasteful: many different overall parenthesizations share the exact same left or right sub-expression, and re-evaluating that shared sub-expression from scratch each time repeats work.

The divide-and-conquer reformulation: instead of generating full shapes, recursively define solve(substring) as the list of every possible value that substring could evaluate to, by trying every operator within it as the "last applied," splitting into left and right, and combining their recursively-computed value lists.

Adding memoization: since solve() is called on OVERLAPPING substrings across different recursive paths, caching results by the substring itself avoids recomputing identical subproblems.

The core idea: divide and conquer directly on the substring (not on full parenthesization shapes), memoized by substring, is both a cleaner formulation and avoids redundant work.

Recursively define solve(substring): if it is purely digits, return that number as the only possible value. Otherwise, for each operator position, recursively solve the left and right substrings, combine every pair of their results using that operator, and collect all such combined values, memoizing by substring.

blocks.caption: Each operator position splits the expression; recursively combine memoized left/right results

blocks.text: Every valid parenthesization of the expression corresponds to some choice of which operator is applied last, at the outermost level, which splits the expression into a left and right sub-expression. Since these sub-expressions are strictly shorter, recursively solving them (and combining every pair of their results with the splitting operator) correctly enumerates every possible value the full expression could take. Memoizing by the exact substring ensures that if the same sub-expression arises via different split paths, its result list is computed only once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: bounded by the Catalan number of ways to parenthesize (exponential in operator count), but memoization avoids recomputation of shared substrings, keeping actual work proportional to the number of DISTINCT substrings encountered times combination cost.
Space: O(number of distinct substrings times average result list size) for the memo table.

blocks.text: Different Ways to Add Parentheses is a classic divide-and-conquer-plus-memoization problem: splitting at every operator as the "last applied" one, recursing on both halves, and reusing results for identical substrings.

items: Forgetting the base case (a pure-digit substring returns that number as its only possible value), causing infinite recursion or missing single-number sub-expressions.
Not memoizing, leading to redundant recomputation of the same substring across different split paths in longer expressions.

blocks.text: Explicitly framing this as "choose which operator is applied LAST, recursively split, and combine," rather than trying to enumerate parenthesized strings directly, demonstrates the divide-and-conquer insight clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "every way of grouping an expression with parentheses", think: divide at each operator (as the last applied), recurse on both sides, combine, memoize by substring.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches share an inherently exponential worst-case bound tied to the Catalan numbers, but memoizing by substring avoids redundant recomputation of shared sub-expressions, making the divide-and-conquer approach the practical standard.

items: Pattern: divide and conquer on substrings, splitting at every operator as the "last applied," combined with memoization.
Core Idea: recursively solve left and right substrings for every operator split, combine every pair of results with that operator, memoize by substring to avoid recomputation.
Time: exponential (Catalan-bounded) for both, but memoization avoids redundant recomputation of shared substrings.
Space: exponential for the naive shape-generation approach, O(distinct substrings) for the memoized approach.
Most Important Observation: every parenthesization corresponds to choosing an operator to apply last, which cleanly splits the problem into two smaller recursive subproblems.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known divide-and-conquer problem closely related to Catalan-number counting problems.
One line memory trick: split at each operator, recurse both sides, combine every pair, memoize by substring.
